questions.prompt: What problem does Chapter 7 identify before it focuses on listening?
choices: People never ask enough questions
Conversations thin out when both people keep trying to perform
Silence is always the main danger

explanation.gentle: The chapter begins with performance pressure inside conversation.
explanation.direct: Option B fits. Carnegie is trying to solve a room crowded by self-display.
explanation.competitive: A talk gets thin when everyone keeps auditioning.

questions.prompt: Why does listening help conversation continue under Carnegie's logic?
choices: Because it gives the other person room to keep unfolding what matters
Because silence is automatically interesting
Because it prevents the listener from ever responding

explanation.gentle: Listening helps because the other person feels more received and keeps going.
explanation.direct: Correct. Attention creates conversational room and lowers strain.
explanation.competitive: Listening gives the talk more oxygen.

questions.prompt: What makes a follow-up question strong in this chapter?
choices: It comes from what the other person just said
It sounds clever and surprising
It avoids personal topics completely

explanation.gentle: The chapter treats real follow-up as something that grows from the answer that just arrived.
explanation.direct: Option A is the key. Active listening produces stronger questions than scripts do.
explanation.competitive: A live follow-up proves the last turn landed.

questions.prompt: Priya is in a meeting and feels herself preparing a smart point while a teammate is still explaining a blocker. Which move best fits Chapter 7?
choices: Hold the point and follow the blocker until the next question grows from it
Interrupt quickly so the room sees she is engaged
Stay silent for the rest of the meeting

explanation.gentle: Chapter 7 asks Priya to let listening shape the next turn rather than rushing to perform.
explanation.direct: Option A fits. The conversation improves when the response grows from the live thread.
explanation.competitive: Track the thread before you chase the spotlight.

questions.prompt: Why might a study-group conversation feel unusually alive under this chapter's logic?
choices: Because one person keeps changing topics so nobody gets stuck
Because someone listens closely enough that the follow-ups come from the answers
Because nobody shares any opinions

explanation.gentle: The chapter says conversations stay alive when answers shape the next turn.
explanation.direct: Correct. Thread-tracking matters more than constant topic changes.
explanation.competitive: The room breathes when reception outruns performance.

questions.prompt: In a personal conversation, what often changes when someone follows the other person's thread instead of reclaiming the floor with a matching story?
choices: The talk usually gains room and feels less competitive
The conversation becomes one-sided and unusable
The other person stops talking because there is less entertainment

explanation.gentle: Listening can make the other person feel more fully received, so the talk opens up.
explanation.direct: Option A matches the chapter. Following the thread reduces strain and keeps the exchange real.

questions.prompt: What keeps question-asking from becoming fake in this chapter?
choices: Using as many questions as possible
Letting the answer genuinely shape the next turn
Keeping all questions emotionally neutral

explanation.gentle: A question stays real when the answer actually lands and changes the conversation.
explanation.direct: Option B preserves the chapter's boundary. Reception matters more than question volume.
explanation.competitive: If the answer changes nothing, the question was theater.

questions.prompt: What weak reading of Chapter 7 does the prose reject?
choices: That good conversation is mostly about passive silence or canned prompts
That people enjoy being listened to
That follow-up questions can matter

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps its focus on active listening rather than on quietness alone or stock questions.
explanation.direct: Option A is the misreading. Carnegie is not teaching blank silence or script maintenance.
explanation.competitive: Silence alone and question theater both miss the point.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between real listening and question theater?
choices: Real listening receives the answer; question theater keeps the form of conversation without the reception
Question theater is stronger because it keeps things moving
There is no real difference if the questions are polite

explanation.gentle: The chapter trusts actual reception more than conversational motion by itself.
explanation.direct: Correct. The form of conversation can survive after its reality drains out.
explanation.competitive: One creates room. The other only preserves the shell.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate high-level summary of Chapter 7?
choices: Good conversation comes mainly from having better stories
Good conversation grows when listening gives the other person room to keep unfolding what matters
Good conversation is safest when you avoid follow-up entirely

explanation.gentle: The chapter makes listening the engine of conversational room.
explanation.direct: Option B is the chapter in one line. Real attention creates better conversation than self-display does.
explanation.competitive: The talk gets better when reception wins more turns than ego.
